title: Complexity Theory
description: What running time means and where the hard limits lie: Big-O through P vs NP.

entries.title: Big-O Notation
entries.summary: Big-O describes how runtime grows as input grows, dropping constants and lower terms. It compares algorithms at scale, where growth dominates hardware.
recognize: Estimating if a solution fits limits
entries.how_it_works: f(n) is O(g(n)) if f(n) <= c*g(n) for all large n. Analyze loops by multiplication, branches by maximum, and repeated work by summation. 1e8 simple ops per second is the standard contest budget.
entries.example:
# n = len(a)
for x in a:      # n times
    for y in a:  # n times each
        pass      # total Theta(n^2)
# Halving loop: while n: n //= 2  -> Theta(log n)
pitfalls: Confusing worst case with Big-O (it bounds any case you state)
Ignoring hidden constants in practice
n=10 needs no analysis; n=1e5 needs it
tips: Budget: 1e8 ops/sec, 256MB
Multiply nested loops, add sequential ones
State which case (worst/average) your bound is for

entries.title: Omega and Theta
entries.summary: Omega gives lower bounds (at least this slow) and Theta gives tight bounds (both sides). Big-O alone only promises 'no worse than'.
recognize: Proving a problem needs at least some work
Distinguishing upper vs lower bound claims
entries.how_it_works: f is Omega(g) if f >= c*g eventually; Theta means both O and Omega. Comparison sorting is Theta(n log n) worst-case: O from merge sort, Omega from decision-tree counting.
entries.example:
# Sorting lower bound idea:
# n! possible orders need log2(n!) = Theta(n log n)
# comparisons to distinguish -> sorting is Omega(n log n)
pitfalls: Saying 'best case O(n)' when you mean Omega
Lower bounds need a model (comparisons? operations?)
Theta requires matching upper and lower proofs
tips: Decision trees prove comparison-sorting lower bounds
Adversary arguments prove other lower bounds
Name the bound type explicitly in writeups

entries.title: Amortized Analysis
entries.summary: Average cost per operation over a sequence, even though single operations can be expensive. Dynamic arrays, union-find, and splay trees are analyzed this way.
recognize: Occasional expensive op among cheap ones
entries.how_it_works: Aggregate method: total cost / n. Or the potential method: charge each op its real cost plus potential change; expensive ops consume banked potential. Doubling array: n appends cost O(n) total because copies halve geometrically.

complexity.time: O(1) amortized append; varies by structure

entries.example:
# Doubling array: appends 1..n cost sum of copies
# copies at sizes 1,2,4,... <= 2n total -> O(1) amortized
# Potential Phi = 2*size - capacity also proves it
pitfalls: Amortized is not average-case (no randomness assumed)
Single-op worst case still matters for latency
Wrong potential function proves nothing
tips: Aggregate counting is usually simplest
Potential = banked work for future expensive ops
Union-find's alpha(n) is amortized

entries.title: Master Theorem
entries.summary: Closed form for recurrences T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n): compare f(n) against n^(log_b a) to read off the answer. It prices most divide-and-conquer at a glance.
entries.how_it_works: Leaves cost n^(log_b a); compare with the root/level work f(n). If f is polynomially smaller, leaves dominate; if larger, the root work dominates; if equal, pay an extra log factor.
entries.example:
# Merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)
# log_2(2) = 1, f(n) = Theta(n^1) -> Case 2
# Answer: Theta(n log n)
# Binary search: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) -> Theta(log n)
pitfalls: Non-constant b or non-polynomial gaps (use Akra-Bazzi)
Floors/ceilings ignored only asymptotically
Forgetting the regularity condition in case 3
tips: Draw the recursion tree to double-check
Akra-Bazzi generalizes to uneven splits
Strassen 7T(n/2)+O(n^2) -> Theta(n^log2(7))

entries.title: Time-Space Tradeoffs
entries.summary: Memory buys speed (memoization, lookup tables) and recomputation saves memory (Hirschberg, streaming). Naming the tradeoff explicitly guides design under limits.
entries.how_it_works: Store results to avoid recompute (DP tables, caches), or recompute to fit memory (rolling arrays keep two DP rows; Hirschberg recovers alignment in linear space). Bitsets compress boolean DP by 64x.

complexity.time: Varies; memory often drops a dimension
complexity.space: O(n) instead of O(n^2) typical win

pitfalls: Rolling arrays destroy reconstruction info (store parents)
Bitset direction mistakes
Cache size: O(n) memory can still TLE on access pattern
tips: Two rows suffice for iterative DP depending only on previous row
Bitset DP for subset-sum is dramatically faster
Hirschberg for linear-space LCS alignment

entries.title: P vs NP
entries.summary: P: solvable fast. NP: verifiable fast. Whether solving is as easy as verifying is the open P vs NP question — the deepest unsolved problem in computer science.
recognize: Understanding why some problems resist fast solutions
entries.how_it_works: A problem is in NP if a claimed solution can be checked in polynomial time (e.g. a proposed tour, a coloring). P ⊆ NP trivially. No proof separates or equates them; most researchers believe P ≠ NP.
entries.example:
# Verifying is easy, solving is (believed) hard:
# Given a graph + a vertex ordering, checking it is a
# Hamiltonian cycle takes O(n) time.
# Finding one is NP-complete.
pitfalls: NP means verifiable, not 'non-polynomial'
NP-hard vs NP-complete are different claims
Assuming P ≠ NP is proven
tips: Membership in NP: exhibit the certificate + checker
NP-hardness: reduce FROM a known hard problem
See th.np-completeness and th.reductions next

entries.title: NP-Completeness
entries.summary: NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP: every NP problem reduces to them. A fast solver for one would collapse all of NP into P.
entries.how_it_works: Cook-Levin: SAT is NP-complete (circuits encode computation). New problems join by reduction from a known NP-complete one, preserving yes/no answers in polynomial time, plus showing membership in NP.
entries.example:
# Canonical NP-complete set (know several cold):
# SAT, 3-SAT, CLIQUE, INDEPENDENT SET,
# VERTEX COVER, HAMILTONIAN CYCLE/PATH,
# TSP decision, SUBSET SUM, KNAPSACK decision,
# 3-COLORING, PARTITION
pitfalls: Reducing the WRONG direction (must go known-hard -> new)
Forgetting the in-NP membership half
Confusing NP-hard (no membership needed) with NP-complete
tips: Learn 3-4 reductions deeply, not 20 shallowly
Decision versions for hardness, optimization for practice
Pseudopolynomial (knapsack) does not mean P

entries.title: Reductions
entries.summary: A polynomial reduction transforms problem A into B preserving answers, proving B is at least as hard as A. The direction — known-hard to new — is the whole game.
recognize: Showing a new problem is hard
entries.how_it_works: Map instances of known-hard A to instances of B in polynomial time such that yes maps to yes and no to no. Gadgets encode A's structure (e.g. SAT variables as graph widgets for 3-coloring). Then B is NP-hard; add in-NP for completeness.

complexity.time: Reduction must run in polynomial time

entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE classic chain:
  SAT -> 3-SAT (split long clauses with fresh variables)
  3-SAT -> CLIQUE (literal-nodes, edges for compatible literals;
                    k-clique <=> satisfiable with k clauses)
  CLIQUE -> INDEPENDENT SET (complement graph)
  INDEPENDENT SET -> VERTEX COVER (complement vertices)
pitfalls: Backward direction proves nothing about the new problem
Exponential-size gadgets invalidate the proof
Forgetting to prove the iff on instances
tips: Memorize the SAT->3SAT->CLIQUE->IS->VC chain
Gadgets are local widgets with global consequences
Draw the construction on a 2-variable example

entries.title: NP-Complete Problem Zoo
entries.summary: The working catalog: SAT family, graph problems (Clique, Vertex Cover, Hamiltonian, Coloring), number problems (Subset Sum, Knapsack, Partition), and TSP. Recognizing disguised members saves hours.
entries.how_it_works: Karp's 21 problems anchor the zoo; each captures a combinatorial essence (choice, ordering, partition). New problems usually match one essence: map your entities to its entities and check the reduction direction.

complexity.time: Exponential exact algorithms (often O(1.3^n)-style); pseudopolynomial for some

entries.example:
# Quick recognition map:
# conflicts/selection -> CLIQUE / INDEPENDENT SET
# cover everything cheaply -> VERTEX COVER / SET COVER
# visit-all route -> HAMILTONIAN / TSP
# split numbers evenly -> PARTITION / SUBSET SUM
# schedule with constraints -> GRAPH COLORING
pitfalls: Pseudopolynomial != polynomial (knapsack, subset sum)
Approximation exists for some (see th.approximation)
Fixed-parameter tractability rescues small parameters
tips: Match the essence, then construct the reduction
Check constraints: small k hints FPT, small W hints pseudopolynomial
See th.approximation when exact is hopeless

entries.title: Approximation Algorithms
entries.summary: When exact is intractable, guarantee near-optimal fast: vertex cover 2-approx by maximal matching, metric TSP 1.5 via Christofides, knapsack FPTAS. Ratios are proven, not hoped.
entries.how_it_works: Design + charging argument: maximal matching edges force OPT to spend >=1 per edge while the algorithm spends 2 (ratio 2). Christofides: MST + matching on odd vertices + shortcutting yields <= 1.5 OPT on metric instances. Scaling + DP gives knapsack's (1-eps) FPTAS.
pitfalls: Ratio direction (maximization vs minimization)
Metric assumption for TSP bounds
Heuristics without ratios are not approximation algorithms
tips: Greedy + charging is the standard proof pattern
LP rounding is the systematic upgrade path
Inapproximability (PCP) bounds how far this goes

entries.title: Randomized Algorithms
entries.summary: Monte Carlo (maybe wrong, fast) vs Las Vegas (always right, random runtime). Quicksort, Karger min-cut, and Miller-Rabin show randomness buying simplicity or speed.
entries.how_it_works: Monte Carlo errs with probability p; k independent runs cut error to p^k. Las Vegas (random quicksort) is always correct with expected-time bounds. Karger contracts random edges; repeating O(n^2 log n) times finds the min cut w.h.p.
entries.example:
# Freivalds check: is A*B == C?
import random
def freivalds(A, B, C, trials=20):
    n = len(A)
    for _ in range(trials):
        r = [random.randint(0, 1) for _ in range(n)]
        # compare A*(B*r) vs C*r in O(n^2)
        Br = [sum(B[i][j] * r[j] for j in range(n)) for i in range(n)]
        ABr = [sum(A[i][j] * Br[j] for j in range(n)) for i in range(n)]
        Cr = [sum(C[i][j] * r[j] for j in range(n)) for i in range(n)]
        if ABr != Cr:
            return False
    return True  # correct w.h.p.
pitfalls: One-sided vs two-sided error confusion
Non-independent repetitions don't amplify
Randomized != heuristic (bounds still proven)
tips: Repeat to amplify; error decays exponentially
Hashing turns worst cases into expected cases
Derandomization is a whole subfield (see also: deterministic fallback)

entries.title: Undecidability and Halting
entries.summary: Some problems admit no algorithm at all: the Halting problem is undecidable by diagonalization, and reductions spread undecidability (Rice's theorem: all nontrivial semantic properties).
entries.how_it_works: Assume a halts() decider; build a program doing the opposite of what halts() predicts about it — contradiction. To show X undecidable, reduce Halting to X: a decider for X would decide Halting. Rice: any nontrivial behavior property is undecidable.
entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE diagonalization:
  assume halts(P, x) decides termination
  define D(P): if halts(P, P): loop forever; else: halt
  ask halts(D, D):
    True  -> D loops -> should be False
    False -> D halts -> should be True
  contradiction, so halts() cannot exist
pitfalls: Undecidable != hard (hard problems still have algorithms)
Reductions go Halting -> new problem
Trivial properties (e.g. 'has 5 states') are decidable
tips: Diagonalization is the core proof move
Rice's theorem shortcuts many behavior questions
Separate complexity (hard) from computability (impossible)
